reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Neurocutaneous Disorders (current reference texts)
clinicalPearls: A congenital organoid hamartoma of the epidermis and adnexa, typically presenting as a hairless yellow-orange plaque on the scalp or face
It is a mosaic lesion caused by post-zygotic activating RAS-pathway variants, usually HRAS and less often KRAS
The lesion evolves with age, becoming smooth and flat in infancy, then verrucous and nodular around puberty under hormonal influence
The characteristic scalp lesion is associated with overlying alopecia because normal follicles are absent
It carries a lifelong risk of secondary tumours, most commonly benign trichoblastoma and syringocystadenoma papilliferum, with basal cell carcinoma the main malignant concern
Extensive lesions may be part of Schimmelpenning syndrome with cerebral, ocular and skeletal anomalies, so wide involvement prompts systemic assessment
Management is generic: observation with clinical surveillance, and consideration of complete excision where there is cosmetic concern or a suspicious secondary growth
reference.pathophysiology: Naevus sebaceus of Jadassohn is a mosaic organoid hamartoma resulting from a post-zygotic activating variant in the RAS-MAPK pathway, most often HRAS and occasionally KRAS, arising in an epidermal progenitor during development. The affected clone produces disordered overgrowth of the epidermis together with sebaceous glands, abortive hair follicles and apocrine structures, giving the lesion its organoid character and its distribution along the lines of Blaschko. Persistent RAS-pathway activation drives the pubertal thickening of the lesion and predisposes to the development of secondary benign and, less commonly, malignant appendageal tumours over the patient's lifetime.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical and dermoscopic assessment of the plaque
Skin biopsy where diagnosis is uncertain or a secondary tumour is suspected
Histopathology of any excised lesion to identify secondary neoplasia
MRI of the brain where the naevus is extensive or neurological features suggest Schimmelpenning syndrome
Ophthalmological review in extensive head-and-neck disease
Molecular testing of lesional tissue for HRAS/KRAS variants where available
redFlags: New nodule, ulceration or bleeding within the plaque suggesting a secondary malignancy
Rapid change in a long-stable lesion
Extensive lesions with seizures or developmental delay indicating a neurocutaneous syndrome
Ocular or skeletal anomalies in association with a large naevus
reference.prognosis: Isolated naevus sebaceus has an excellent prognosis; the main long-term consideration is the modest risk of secondary tumours, predominantly benign, so periodic surveillance or elective excision is reasonable, while extensive lesions require assessment for associated syndromic disease.
pitfalls: Assuming any secondary growth is malignant when benign trichoblastoma is far more common
Failing to reassess a lesion that changes in adulthood
Not screening for systemic involvement when the naevus is extensive
Excising purely for a low malignancy risk without discussing that benign tumours predominate
references: Happle R. Mosaicism in Human Skin
management: Manage isolated, asymptomatic lesions by periodic clinical and dermoscopic surveillance, counselling that the mosaic RAS-pathway lesion is benign but carries a lifelong risk of secondary appendageal tumours.
Offer elective full-thickness surgical excision for cosmetic concern, symptomatic lesions or where reliable surveillance is impractical, sending the specimen for histopathology.

Promptly biopsy or excise any new nodule, ulceration, bleeding or accelerated growth to exclude secondary neoplasia, commonly benign trichoblastoma or syringocystadenoma papilliferum and less often basal cell carcinoma.
Time excision with awareness of pubertal thickening, and counsel on the associated localised alopecia over scalp lesions and on scarring or reconstruction where relevant.
Assess extensive or multiple lesions for Schimmelpenning syndrome, arranging brain MRI and neurological review where cerebral involvement or seizures are suspected.
Arrange ophthalmological review for extensive head-and-neck disease and paediatric developmental assessment as part of syndromic evaluation.
Explain the post-zygotic mosaic aetiology when counselling families: the lesion is not inherited and recurrence risk in future pregnancies is not increased.
